title: How I Approached Code 365
excerpt: A walkthrough of the user and admin flows behind Code 365, from browser requests to data, analytics, and deployment logs.
imageCaption: The user flow traces a request from the browser through Code 365 services to the database.
body: Building Code 365 meant thinking through two connected paths: how a learner uses the product and how the application is operated. These diagrams show the request path through the user-facing application, then the admin and monitoring connections that support the service.

content.text: User flow: from the browser to the database

A learner starts in the browser and uses the React frontend to browse learning paths, solve problems, or check progress. The frontend sends requests to API routes hosted on Vercel. Authentication is handled through Supabase Auth, and authenticated requests can read or update the learner’s data in PostgreSQL through the database service.

content.alt: Code 365 user flow diagram showing a learner using the React frontend, Vercel API routes, Supabase authentication, and PostgreSQL database
content.caption: User flow: the frontend, API routes, authentication, and database work together to serve a learner’s request.

content.text: Admin flow: manage data and monitor the service

The admin side has a separate route to PostgreSQL for database updates. The diagram also shows operational visibility around the application: Google Analytics receives event and query data, while Vercel provides page insights and deployment logs. This makes data management and service monitoring part of the overall system design.

content.alt: Code 365 admin flow diagram showing admin database updates, Google Analytics events and query logs, and Vercel page insights and deployment logs
content.caption: Admin flow: database updates and monitoring connect the platform to its operational tools.

content.text: Together, the diagrams show the two sides I considered while building Code 365: a direct path for learners to use the product, and clear connections for managing data and understanding how the service is running. The platform is available at code365.tech.

title: Building Smart Mart: My First Full-Stack Project
excerpt: What I learned building an ecommerce application across the frontend, backend, database, and admin workflows.
imageCaption: The product catalog is the starting point for the Smart Mart shopping journey.
body: Smart Mart was my first full-stack project, built as a learning project rather than freelance work. I wanted to understand how a complete ecommerce application fits together, from the interface shoppers use to the services and data behind it.

Working across the Angular frontend, Spring Boot backend, database, and admin screens taught me to think beyond individual pages. A product, cart, and order each need to stay connected as a customer moves through the shopping flow.

content.text: I built the product experience around a familiar path: browse and filter the catalog, save items to a wishlist or add them to the cart, then review the order before checkout. The project also includes customer registration and login, order history, and invoice generation.

content.alt: Smart Mart storefront showing a filterable product catalog
content.caption: The catalog gives shoppers a place to search and explore products.

content.text: The frontend uses Angular and Angular Material, with Spring Boot and Hibernate handling backend services and persistence. Connecting those layers helped me understand how a shopper’s actions become authenticated requests and changes to product, cart, and order data. The application supports MySQL or PostgreSQL and uses JWT-based authentication.

content.alt: Smart Mart shopping cart with quantities, order summary, shipping address, and checkout
content.caption: The cart brings selected products and order totals together before checkout.

content.text: Build for the customer and the admin

An ecommerce flow continues after payment. Customers can review orders and follow their status, while admin views support product and order management. Building both sides helped me see how the same order data serves different needs across the application.

content.alt: Smart Mart admin orders table showing customer, product, payment amount, quantity, and order status
content.caption: The admin order view supports reviewing orders and updating fulfillment status.

content.text: Smart Mart was an important first step in my full-stack development journey. It gave me hands-on experience bringing a storefront, backend services, authentication, database persistence, checkout, and administration into one working project.

title: Improving RAG search quality for AI applications
excerpt: A practical framework for better retrieval augmented generation: chunking, metadata, reranking, and evaluation.
imageCaption: Good retrieval gives a language model the right context at the right time.
body: Most RAG problems are retrieval problems before they are generation problems. If the right source never reaches the context window, a stronger model will not reliably fix the answer.

Start with clean documents, useful metadata, and chunks that preserve meaning. Measure recall with a small set of questions from real users, then add hybrid search or reranking only when the evaluation shows a gap.
Finally, design for citation and correction. Let people inspect the source behind an answer, report a bad result, and improve the corpus over time.

title: A practical guide to AI agents in production
excerpt: How to design reliable AI agents with tools, guardrails, evaluation, and human control.
imageCaption: Production agents need observable steps, not just fluent answers.
body: AI agents are most useful when they complete a bounded workflow instead of pretending to be universal experts. Start with the user outcome, map the decisions the agent must make, and keep each tool call explicit.

Reliability comes from the system around the model: typed inputs, permission checks, retries, timeouts, structured outputs, and evaluations built from real tasks. A polished chat surface cannot compensate for invisible failure modes.
The best agent UX keeps people informed. Show what the agent is doing, make approvals meaningful, and provide a clear recovery path when a tool or model is uncertain.

title: The quiet power of building in public
excerpt: What changes when you share the process, not just the polished result.
imageCaption: A working archive is often more useful than a polished announcement.
body: The internet rewards finished things. Launch posts, tidy case studies, the neat version of a long and complicated process. But most of the useful thinking happens before the reveal.

Building in public has become a way to make that thinking visible. It is not about turning every work session into content. It is about leaving enough of a trail that other people can learn from the decisions, mistakes, and small discoveries along the way.
For me, the best kind of sharing is specific and honest: a screenshot of an awkward first pass, a short note about a technical trade-off, or a post-mortem that says what I would do differently.

title: What I learned shipping my first AI product
excerpt: Useful AI products start with a clear job, trustworthy UX, and a feedback loop—not an impressive demo.
imageCaption: Good AI products make trust visible in the interface.
body: The first prototype was impressive for about five minutes. It could summarize, brainstorm, and answer questions. Then the novelty wore off and the real question arrived: what job does this actually help someone do?
The strongest lesson was to narrow the product until the value became obvious. A focused workflow with a fast feedback loop beat a general assistant with a longer feature list every time.

The technical pieces matter, but trust matters more. Good defaults, visible sources, graceful failure states, and an interface that lets people stay in control are the difference between a model demo and a product people return to.

title: A practical guide to better interfaces
excerpt: A few small principles I return to whenever a screen feels almost right.
imageCaption: Hierarchy gives every interface a clear point of view.
body: Good interfaces rarely announce themselves. They reduce the amount of thinking required to move through a task, and they make the next useful action feel natural.

Start with hierarchy. If everything is loud, nothing is clear. Give the primary action space, keep supporting information close to the thing it explains, and let typography do more of the work than decoration.
Then test the edges: empty states, long names, slow networks, keyboard navigation, and the moment after an action succeeds.
